result.summary: The hymn opens by praising Dionysus, son of Zeus and Semele, and tells how the Nymphs raised him in a cave at Nysa. He then roams the woods with the Nymphs following, and the poet closes with a prayer for many returning seasons.

scenes.title: Dionysus raised by the Nymphs
scenes.summary: The singer introduces Dionysus, who is nursed by the Nymphs at Nysa and then wanders the wooded glens with them in his train.

scenes.title: Closing prayer to Dionysus
scenes.summary: The poet bids the god farewell and asks to return rejoicing to the festival season for many years.

characters.name: Dionysus
characters.description: ivy-crowned god of wine, son of Zeus and Semele

characters.name: Nymphs
characters.description: rich-haired nurses who raised Dionysus at Nysa

notable_quotes.reason: The closing prayer is a typical hymn formula asking for return to the festival in future years.

analysis.text: The hymn presents Dionysus as a nature god, raised among Nymphs and roaming wild woods, linking him with ivy, vines and ecstatic revelry.
Homeric Hymns were short prefaces sung before longer recitations or at festivals; the closing prayer for returning to the season reflects this performance setting.

fun_facts.text: The location of Nysa was never fixed in antiquity; several places from Thrace to Libya to India were claimed as the site.

language_notes.text: "Loud-crying" translates a cult epithet (Greek Eriboas/Bromios type) evoking the shouts of his worshippers and the god's own roaring cry.
"Dells" are small wooded valleys; Nysa is a legendary mountain whose location the ancients placed in several different lands.
"Coombes" are deep wooded valleys or hollows on a hillside.
"A god oft hymned" means a god often praised in song; it is an aside noting his fame.
"This season" refers to the festival at which the hymn is sung; the poet prays to be present at it again in future years.

context_notes.text: Semele was a mortal woman, daughter of Cadmus of Thebes. Dionysus, god of wine and ecstasy, was unusual for having a mortal mother.
Nymphs were female nature spirits of mountains, trees and springs. Here they act as the infant god's nurses.
Dionysus is the god of the vine, so "abundant clusters" refers to grape bunches and the wine harvest.

literary_notes.text: "Ivy-crowned" and "loud-crying" are descriptive epithets that characterize Dionysus through his emblem and his noisy worship.
The forest "filled with their outcry" gives a vivid sound picture of the ecstatic revel band, with the god as leader.
The closing farewell and request for return follows the standard hymn ending, binding the poet's own hope to the god's favor.
